subject: Right truncation based on model fit and/or CV?

messages.author: 4c62fdc31c385890
messages.subject: Right truncation based on model fit and/or CV?
parts:
Dear All, 

I am trying to select a cut-off point for right truncation. My data is from line transects and I want to truncate my observations using more than simply a rule of thumb value (e.g., 10% or 15%) or visual observation of my pdf curve and data histogram.Someone suggest me to decide based on goodness of fit tests like Chi-square, Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises for different percentages of data exclusion (0% to 20% of observations), but the models with the best fits are not always the ones with the lower coefficient of variation. For example, these are some of my models with greater fit p-values for Chi-square and K-S tests (in decreasing order):

  
Here by excluding 9% of observations (first in the list) I get the greater fit (larger p-values for Chi-square GOF and K-S GOF), but the CV is larger than a model with relatively poorer fit, excluding 6% of the data (fourth model in this list). So, in this case what is the best option to choose a right truncation cut off point?

As additional information, distances of all my observations were calculated using a rangefinder and I let the program to select the distance intervals for the histogram . When distances are measured accurately, it is always a good option to let the program define the distance intervals or it is still better to define them manually? This is another doubt I have but also connected as fit is affected with this decision. 

Thanks in advance for any clarification on this matter, or any suggestions.

MSc. Sergio Nolazco
Institute of Biosciences
University of Sao Paulo
Brazil

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Right truncation based on model fit and/or CV?
parts:
Sergio, once you have a good fit to your data (say p-value above 0.1), using GoF to decide on the best truncation distance is not a good strategy – it will tend to truncate too many data.  (You can see this if you try much greater truncation – as you delete data, usually, the model will be able to match the remaining data more closely – because you are reducing the amount of random variation.)  So a good fit combined with a low cv is a sensible strategy.  I tend to favour less truncation rather than more, provided the fit is good.

 

If you have no rounding at all in your data, it should make very little difference if you allow Distance to select intervals.  In songbird surveys in woodland for example, most detections are aural, and then you have to judge position relative to the location that you measure with the rangefinder, so that rounding can still occur.  In that case, I would manually select cutpoints.

 

Steve Buckland
